title: MLB tells veteran umpire he went too far by policing a rookie’s tilted cap: Sources
content:
The apology umpire Doug Eddings issued to St. Louis Cardinals rookie reliever Hancel Rincon on Saturday came after Major League Baseball communicated to the veteran ump that he acted inappropriately the previous night when he told the rookie reliever to straighten his cap.

Umpires operate with broad discretion if they believe a player’s actions are distracting, but according to two people briefed on the matter who were granted anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly, the league viewed Eddings’ admonishment of Rincon as going too far.

Eddings stopped Rincon on the field in the middle of the first inning of Saturday’s game when the Cardinals relievers were walking to the bullpen. Rincon took the exchange as an apology for an that incident drew intense attention throughout the sport, with the umpire’s actions triggering a wave of backlash.

“Saturday’s gesture of apology by Doug on the field speaks for itself,” a league spokesperson told The Athletic.

It’s unclear whether Eddings will face further discipline from MLB.

Rincon, 24, was making his major-league debut Friday night when, on a 2-0 count with one out in the sixth inning, Eddings instructed Cardinals catcher Leo Bernal, another rookie, to tell the pitcher to adjust his cap.

Eddings, the crew chief and plate umpire in that game, told two reporters afterward that he acted after a Rockies hitter asked if Rincon was allowed to wear his cap tilted. A Rockies staffer, granted anonymity for his candor, disputed that account, saying none of the team’s hitters mentioned Rincon’s cap.

Eddings also acknowledged that no rule exists requiring players to wear their caps a certain way.

Regardless of how it began, the incident led to the ejection of Cardinals manager Oli Marmol, who contended that Eddings exerted his authority in an extreme and unnecessary fashion.

The strong feelings spilled over into the following night. Before Saturday’s game, both Marmol and Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer engaged in lengthy conversations with Eddings, and many Cardinals players wore their hats askew.

The included Rincon, who surrendered four runs on two hits in one-plus innings, all while wearing a tilted cap, though this time he was not asked to straighten it.

Rincon, a native of the Dominican Republic, told reporters he did not understand everything Eddings said during their brief conversation on the field between innings, which was captured by the Cardinals’ broadcast. Spanish is Rincon’s first language, and the two spoke without an interpreter. But the pitcher said he was under the impression that Eddings was sorry, and appreciated the umpire’s good wishes.

“I understood a couple words, and it looked like he apologized to me for what happened last night,” Rincon said. “He also told me good luck with the rest of my career as a big leaguer. I told him, don’t worry, it’s nothing personal, and everything stays here.”

The Cardinals on Sunday optioned Rincon to Triple-A Memphis.
